newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Crisis is time to lend to Russia -- IMF head.
newsitem.headline: Crisis is time to lend to Russia -- IMF head.

text.p: The head of the International Monetary Fund, in Moscow for official talks, said Wednesday that the time had come to resume lending to Russia, even though its economy was still in crisis.

IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said Russia's economy, which shrank by 6 percent last year, could show 6 percent growth by the turn of the century and inflation could be at single-digit rates -- as in "other industrial countries" -- next year.

"Stabilization is proceeding in a remarkable way," he said but added: "Russia risks being mired in this economic no man's land between a centrally planned system and a fully functioning market economy."

Camdessus reminded students at an international affairs institute that the fund had granted Russia a $10 billion, three-year Extended Fund Facility Loan last year, when conditions were worse than they are now.
"Why would we shy away now from continuing extending our support to Russia?" he asked.

"This is also the time for us in the international community to go ahead with our support for the completion of your reforms ... by resuming our financing and risking our resources once again in support of your program: a signal the markets expect, a signal your programme deserves," he said.

The IMF has repeatedly suspended monthly payments of the loan -- one of the reasons that Camdessus was in Moscow for talks with government officials -- and fears that tax revenues are running well below budgeted levels could undermine public finances.
Low tax revenues are preventing the government from paying wages and pensions, a major social-economic problem, he said.
Leonid Abalkin, an economist-reformer who advised former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, said Russia had forced down inflation at the cost of not paying wages and pensions.

Russia had built up some 64 trillion roubles ($11 billion) in wage and pension arrears by the end of 1996 and this shortage of cash dampened official inflation to 18 percent year-on-year in February, Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital investment bank in Moscow, said he had not seen any indications that conditions had improved since the IMF declined to issue an intallment on the loan last month.
"Structural reforms may have begun but not much progress appears to have been made. Budget targets are in danger of being missed," he said.
Camdessus referred to Russia's current situation as a crisis and blasted government corruption and structural weaknesses which allowed massive tax evasion.

Tax evasion, close ties between government and certain companies and the need for efficient tax, judicial and police structures should be major targets for reformers, he said, calling government corruption "absolutely unacceptable."
Camdessus credited President Boris Yeltsin and his new team, a young group of reformers appointed in a cabinet shake-up last month, with understanding problems but said he was looking for results.

"I perceive a renewed emphasis on reforms ... but it remains surprising that not a single bankruptcy has occurred among major tax offenders, as would have been the case in a properly working market economy."
Investors were also watching for concrete improvements, he said.

"Russia's declining rate of domestic investment, sluggish rate of foreign investment and rising share of activity in the gray market are all clear signals that such a framework is not in place," he said.
